title: Flattening the stream of consciousness
takeaway: Projecting the ten most active J-lens directions out of layers L38–54 while the model narrates its own stream of consciousness strips the experiential language from the narration on Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6, while control perturbations of identical magnitude along other directions leave the score near baseline. During ordinary, unablated narration, the workspace itself is dominated by tokens like thinking and feeling — content the model is not about to say.
walkthrough:
The figure has three panels, A, B, and C. Together they run one intervention — suppressing the model's workspace while it narrates its own stream of consciousness — and check what changes in the narration. This is the paper's main evidence for the [[experiential-report-flattening]] result.

Panel A prints two responses from Sonnet 4.5 to the same prompt, one of six such prompts. The first comes from the unmodified model. The second comes from the model under [[j-space-ablation]]: at every position, the ten most active J-lens directions are projected out of the residual stream, in layers L38 through L54. Layer numbers here follow [[layer-percentage-indexing]]: they read as percentages of depth, so this band covers roughly the first third of the [[workspace-layers]]. The setting is deliberately light. Ablating more directions, or later layers, damages coherence before anything subtler can be seen. Under this ablation the model still writes fluently about its own processing, but the register shifts from felt description to mechanical status report.

Panel B quantifies the shift. Each response receives an [[experiential-language-score]]: three binary judgments from an Opus 4.6 [[llm-grader]] — whether the moment is conveyed from the inside rather than observed as a status report, whether the perspective is first-person felt rather than third-person mechanism, and whether the vocabulary is sensory rather than computational — averaged together. Bars show the fraction of responses scored as experiential, by model and condition, with 95% intervals; dots are per-prompt rates. The load-bearing comparison is against [[matched-norm-controls]]: perturbations calibrated to disturb the activations by the same magnitude, at the same layers and positions, but along other directions — a random direction, a shrinking of the non-J-space component of the activation ([[j-space-component]]), or a dampening of the ten most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions. Ablation collapses the score on Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6; the controls stay near baseline. Haiku 4.5 is absent because ablation breaks its coherence before its register changes.

Panel C reads the workspace during the unablated narrations. For each token it shows the fraction of (response position × layer) slots at which that token sits in the top-10 [[j-lens-readout]], over the ablated band (dark) and at the final layer (light); the twenty tokens shown are those most elevated over non-experiential baseline prompts. The contents are dominated by thinking at 58% of slots, thoughts at 23%, feeling at 17%, and conscious at 7% — far more often than these words appear in the model's actual output at the same positions. The workspace is not echoing the text; it holds its own [[metacognitive-representations]] — thinking-and-feeling content the model is not about to say.

terms.definition: A representative pair of transcripts: Sonnet 4.5 answering the same stream-of-consciousness prompt with and without J-space ablation, one of six prompts in the set.
A bar chart of the fraction of responses scored as using experiential language, broken out by model and by condition (baseline, J-space ablation, and the matched-norm controls).
The J-space contents during the unablated narrations: for each of the top 20 tokens, the fraction of (response position × layer) slots where it appears in the top-10 lens readout.
The intervention under test: at each position, the residual stream's projections onto the ten most active J-lens vectors are removed, here in layers L38–54 only.

A control intervention calibrated to perturb the activations by the same magnitude, at the same layers and positions, as the ablation — but along other directions. It tests whether the effect comes from what is removed rather than from how much.
The unmodified model's responses to the same prompts; the condition every intervention is compared against.
The matched-norm control that perturbs the activation along a randomly chosen direction.
The matched-norm control that shrinks the part of the activation lying outside the J-space — the complement of what ablation removes.
The matched-norm control that dampens the activation's projections onto its ten most strongly aligned sparse-autoencoder decoder directions — interpretable features that are not J-lens vectors.
The metric on the y-axis of panel B: the average of three binary LLM-graded judgments of whether a response describes experience from the inside.
An Opus 4.6-based judge scoring each response against a written rubric; three separate rubrics (felt vs. observed, first-person felt perspective, sensory vocabulary) each return 0 or 1.
An open-ended prompt asking the model to narrate its ongoing experience; the prompt family this figure's responses come from.
The mid-size Claude model whose transcripts appear in panel A and whose scores appear in panel B; the effect is strongest and most examined here.
A larger Claude model included in panel B; ablation reduces its experiential language score the same way.
The largest and newest model in panel B, which shows the same reduction; a separate instance of it also serves as the grader.
The smallest Claude tier, absent from the figure: on it, J-space ablation degrades coherence before producing any qualitative change in the reports.
The ablated layer band. Layer numbers are percentages of model depth under the paper's 0–100 reindexing, so this is the band from 38% to 54% of depth — the first third of the workspace range.
The last layer of the model, shown as the light bars in panel C for contrast: readouts there track what the model is about to say, unlike the workspace band.
The ten highest-scoring vocabulary tokens when an activation is passed through the J-lens; panel C counts how often each token is among them.
The unit panel C's fractions are over: every combination of a token position in the response and a layer in the range considered counts as one slot.
The tokens dominating the workspace during narration — concepts of mental activity itself, present in the lens far more often than in the model's actual output at the same positions.

terms.term: top 20 by increase over baseline prompts
terms.definition: The selection rule for panel C's tokens: the twenty tokens whose top-10 lens occupancy rises most relative to prompts unrelated to experience, filtering out tokens common everywhere.
The uncertainty ranges on panel B's bars; the paper's success-rate error bars elsewhere are Wilson 95% intervals for a proportion.
Individual points over each bar in panel B, one per prompt, showing how the scored fraction varies across the prompt set.
Dark bars count slots within the ablated layers L38–54; light bars count slots at the final layer only.
The number of top J-lens directions projected out per position — 10 here; larger values impair response coherence.

numbers.meaning: k, the number of most-active J-lens directions ablated at each position; also the size of the top-k readout list panel C counts membership in. Chosen because larger k tends to impair coherence.
The ablated layer band, in percent-of-depth indexing: the first third of the workspace range. Later layer ranges also impair coherence, so the ablation stays early.

Three binary grader judgments (felt vs. observed, experiential perspective, sensory vocabulary), averaged into the experiential language score; also three models showing the effect, and three matched-norm control types in the main comparison.
Stream-of-consciousness prompts in the set panel A samples from ("one of six prompts shown", per the caption).
The number of stream-of-consciousness prompts the body text says the score reduction is computed across; the caption says six — the paper leaves this one-off discrepancy unexplained.
Fraction of (position × layer) slots at which thinking appears in the top-10 lens readout during unablated narration — the single most dominant workspace token.
Slot fraction for thoughts, the second most dominant token.

Slot fraction for conscious. All four fractions far exceed how often these words appear in the model's output distribution at the same positions, which is the argument that the workspace is not merely echoing the text.
Tokens shown in panel C: the top 20 by increase in lens occupancy over non-experience-related baseline prompts.
Confidence level of panel B's error bars on the scored fractions.
Claude version numbers: Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6 show the flattening; Haiku 4.5 is excluded because ablation breaks its coherence first.
